Assessment: The richest symbolic conversation candidate: concepts, English rule parsing, topics, rejoinders and user facts. C++/JNI, serialized engine access, asset loading and script authoring are substantial work. English rule parsing is model-free; do not assume foreign TreeTagger assets or integrations meet the same constraints.

Recommendation: Prototype first as the simpler engine baseline
Assessment: Java trigger/response scripting with variables, conditions and input/reply history. Suitable for small talk and personality packs. Old default-branch code, so own the maintenance risk; validate Android and R8. Not a general semantic interpreter or ready conversation corpus.
Same scripting family in JS. A useful reference for behavior or newer implementation choices; adds a JS runtime if embedded in native Run. Do not install both Java and JS engines.

Ready AIML small-talk content, optimized for Pandorabots. A compatible local interpreter is required; platform extensions and personality need review. GPL content requires distribution-specific review for proprietary Run. Not a no-effort offline drop-in.

License evidence: MIT-style license text; API reports NOASSERTION
Assessment: AIML 2.1 interpreter and an extensive Python bot platform. Embedded Python use is documented, but the dependency list includes server/channel integrations and optional services. Interpreter license does not clear every bundled AIML file. Too much Android packaging work for its likely benefit.

Recommendation: Study its dialogue design; resolve license before copying
License evidence: setup.py declares MIT; no root license retrieved
Assessment: State-transition dialogue manager with Natex matching/generation, variables and macros. Strong example of mixed-initiative authored conversation. Python and NLTK/macros complicate Android and the no-model boundary; assess the exact enabled macros, not the project label.
Scripted chatbot with topic/conversation facilities, but old JS stack and NLP dependencies need separate review. No demonstrated advantage over the simpler RiveScript baseline for Run.
Archived server/channel bot framework. Helps connect bots to messaging platforms, not Run's offline understanding or local content. Does not supply the missing conversational intelligence.

Recommendation: Do not adopt under current constraints
Assessment: Powerful intent/entity/dialogue framework, normally deployed with trained NLU/dialogue components in Python. Rule-only configurations exist, but adopting that stack does not provide a lightweight no-model Android solution.

Learning/response-selection framework with a typical statistical NLP/training stack. Some adapters can be simple, but that is not an advantage over a controlled native retrieval layer. Evaluate its separately licensed corpus independently.

License evidence: MIT for inspected repository; services separate
Assessment: Current AI-agent/platform ecosystem is centered on LLM/service integrations. Historical Botpress versions have different capabilities and licensing; they are not interchangeable evidence for a current offline solution.

English tokenization, phrase matching and linguistic transformations without requiring a pretrained neural pipeline for its core rule/lexicon approach. Useful normalization reference. JS embedding/porting cost and linguistic mistakes remain; not a coreference or conversation engine.

Recommendation: Do not adopt default NLU stack
Assessment: Default intent manager trains a classifier. Model-free utilities could be isolated, but a full Node/NLU stack conflicts with the current no-trained-model constraint and adds unnecessary runtime complexity.
The documented pipeline loads a language model. Offline execution is not the same as model-free execution. Its tokenizer sibling can be evaluated independently.

Standalone rule-driven tokenizer. Potentially useful for punctuation, token boundaries and mentions, but requires JS or a port and does not solve dialogue state. Prefer native implementation if the gain is small.

Recommendation: Do not adopt model-based NLP pipeline
Assessment: Many useful language tasks require trained models. Some utility pieces may be model-free, but Java alone is not enough to satisfy Run's constraints or prove Android compatibility.
Large NLP pipeline with trained resources and licensing/integration implications. Rule subcomponents do not justify packaging the full system for this app.

Recommendation: Reuse algorithm or a reviewed JVM port
License evidence: MIT code; frequency sources still need provenance
Assessment: Fast typo correction and word segmentation based on dictionary deletes and frequency data. Helpful for misspelled commands. Original is C#, not a native Kotlin dependency. Never silently rewrite task titles, place names, dates or quantities.

Recommendation: Strong date-parser reference; optional JS prototype
Assessment: Calendar/date ranges, reference dates and explicit versus inferred fields. More expressive than scattered date regexes, but JS integration and Run's date policies must be evaluated. Extracting a date does not say whether it belongs to travel, exam or a subtask.

Broad multilingual date parsing in Python. Useful for generating examples and comparison data without deploying Python into Run. Its defaults still need explicit locale, relative-base and future/past policies.

Grammar-based natural-language dates on the JVM. A plausible model-free Java candidate, but very old default-branch code and date/time dependencies need review. Preserve timezone, ambiguous-date and calendar-validity checks around it.

Recommendation: Corpus/rule reference only under strict no-model policy
License evidence: BSD-style with PATENTS file; review exact terms
Assessment: Excellent typed time/number/unit rule corpus, but the tree also contains generated ranking classifiers. Haskell/native packaging is substantial. Do not describe the default system as entirely model-free. Removing ranking would be a separate fork to prove.

Typed date/time, number, unit and related extraction through rule/resource recognizers. Java implementation exists but the README calls it in progress; .NET has primary feature coverage. Java POMs target 8 but include JVM dependencies. An API named Model does not itself imply trained ML weights.

Recommendation: Use only for a deliberately authored grammar
Assessment: Mature parser generator/runtime useful for typed edit commands and compound syntax. It does not come with a complete conversational English grammar. Generated parser code is a runtime cost to evaluate against simpler Kotlin grammar tools.

Recommendation: Alternative grammar library; not first choice
Assessment: PEG/parser-combinator approach for composing grammar rules. Useful alternative to regex sprawl, but Java/Scala tooling and dependencies need review. Not dialogue understanding out of the box.

Contains Kotlin and Swift despite GitHub labeling the repository Swift. Explicit transitions and effects can help ownership. Smaller conceptual fit than a large conversation framework, but advanced history/persistence requirements remain app work.

Kotlin/Android support, guarded/nested states, history and optional event persistence. Core depends on Kotlin stdlib. Useful for pending questions, interruptions and resumption. Verify library/Kotlin version compatibility; Run uses Kotlin 2.0.21. State transitions alone do not interpret text.

Recommendation: Architecture/reference; runtime only if JS is justified
Assessment: Strong statecharts, actors and explicit event handling. Excellent reference for ownership and interruption design. Native Kotlin Run would otherwise acquire a JS runtime just for state management.
Standard XML statecharts and Java execution. Fits explicit dialogue states conceptually, but XML/runtime expression dependencies can be more cumbersome than native Kotlin state management.

Recommendation: Do not add current full runtime by default
Assessment: Strong lexical retrieval and ranking, but inspected mainline build documentation asks for JDK 25. Neither Java branding nor an older release establishes Android support. Run already uses Room 2.6.1; evaluate a Room FTS4 curated-content index first. Android platform SQLite cannot universally be assumed to expose FTS5.

Concept relations can expand topic associations and suggest relevant follow-ups. Full graph/build stack is inappropriate for a phone. Data is noisy, does not establish a fact or task requirement, and requires source attribution. Exclude Numberbatch embeddings under no-model policy.

License evidence: TM-1 through TM-4 READMEs state CC BY 4.0
Assessment: Task-oriented dialogues with corrections and realistic user phrasing. Strong source for conversation scenarios and annotated slots. Not an executable assistant or broad knowledge base. Repository archived; static examples remain useful. Attribute adapted source examples.

Recommendation: Priority reference for multi-domain state and repair
Assessment: Annotated intents, slots, services and state transitions useful for interruption/clarification design. Do not import it as a response brain or assume training scripts fit no-model runtime. Adapted data retains relevant share-alike obligations.

Recommendation: Reference only; no bulk response import
License evidence: Apache-2.0 tooling; each source dataset differs
Assessment: Provides processing recipes for response-selection datasets, not a single uniformly licensed conversation pack. Reddit/subtitle-style data is noisy and often mismatched to a personal assistant. Do not inherit the code license onto source conversations.

Recommendation: Use selected multi-domain examples for design/evaluation
License evidence: MIT at repository root; verify exact dataset/version provenance
Assessment: Useful reference for travel-like slot filling and cross-domain turns. Domains and annotations have limitations; it does not give a general-purpose travel planner or license live factual claims. Data-driven scenario work need not mean training a model.

Classic logic/search/planning implementations for learning and prototyping. No pretrained model is required for symbolic algorithms, but it is not a production Android conversation engine. Do not import an educational framework wholesale.

Constraint programming can improve prerequisite, availability and resource scheduling after text is parsed into data. Current POM targets Java 17; Android/API/dependency behavior must still be proved. Avoid optional native continuous-solver features and bound solve time.
Large planning/optimization framework. Useful modeling references, but footprint, lifecycle and runtime assumptions need review. It cannot interpret conversation or remember dialogue for Run.

Modern scheduling/optimization tooling. README requires Java 21+, and community versus enterprise features differ. Desktop Java/Kotlin support is not Android support. No conversational benefit until structured constraints already exist.

Java dialogue manager with probabilistic rules, Bayesian state and optional learning. Useful blackboard/state concepts, but its probabilistic models, speech plugins and desktop tooling need separate constraint review. No blanket no-model or distribution approval.
Archived browser dialogue/state/blackboard system with Tracery generation. Good examples of separating state from reply text. Not a maintained Android conversation framework.

Separate, user-contributed YAML dialogue corpus. A curated subset can become authored rules without training ChatterBot. Inspect individual files/provenance and rewrite persona, factual claims and generic chains. Broad factual correctness and natural multi-turn context are not guaranteed.

Kotlin parser combinators for composing command/edit grammar into typed results. Can improve add/remove/rename/summary/quantity syntax. We still author grammar and resolve references against the actual dialogue frame; verify current Kotlin artifact compatibility.

Java port of SymSpell; POM targets Java 8. Better packaging candidate than original C# for Run, but dependencies, dictionaries, maintenance and R8 still need checking. Restrict corrections to command vocabulary/high-confidence suggestions.

Recommendation: Reuse constrained generation ideas; JS or native subset
Assessment: Grammar-based text expansion with reusable bindings and variation, without an LLM. Helpful for varied acknowledgements/personality after a response intent is chosen. Does not understand input, maintain true memory or validate facts; do not make all variation random.
